reply_text:
Graph regenerated (giant component 621 → 734). Now tracing where the `@holds-at` markers came from:㊥ (rerun, and where @holds-at came from) I've rerun the graph. The regenerated giant component has 734 of 1,431 patterns, up from 621, and it has 4,552 edges. Most of the new edges are co-cited and next-in-session links from turn analyses written since 30 September. The 52 `@holds-at` markers come in three batches. 18 are the R-number labels from the plop-2026 catalogue, copied onto the `aif/` patterns, so they're as trustworthy as that mapping. The other 34 are weaker, so I'll keep the two groups apart in the comparison.

㊢ (provenance of the 52 markers) Taking each file's first `@holds-at` commit, all in futon3:

| Commit | Date | Markers | What it was |
|---|---|---:|---|
| `2fbb58a` | 30 Aug | 18 | "peg every Figure-4 R-node to a pattern (PREREG-war-machine §1b)". One line per `aif/` mechanism pattern, naming the R-numbered paragraph in `p4ng/sec-catalog.tex`, plus two patterns written for R15 and R20, which the library lacked. The message says that before this, the only link was title similarity. |
| `ccaf363` | 5 Sep | 21 | "L5 problem-node mining": the `problems/rN-…` dossier nodes, one per R-number. They're about the R-node and record the issue against it. |
| `7c3462e`, `2aa8d0c` | 22–25 Aug | 10 | Five `@how` links renamed to `@holds-at` because of a clash with the grammar's own `@how`, plus five problem patterns for the control map's red rings. |
| three single commits | 25 Aug–5 Sep | 3 | One feature spec each for R2 and R8, and one more catalogue problem node. |

All the commits are signed as you, but they were written by agent seats; the `aif/` pegging names claude-15 in the file comments.

🖖 (how I'll use them) There will be up to four association sources, each recorded separately:
1. **Code bids:** done; sparse, mostly on engineering-practice patterns.
2. **Turn bids:** running now.
3. **Graph distance:** from the 18 catalogue `aif/` patterns only.
4. **Graph distance:** from all 52 markers, kept separate so the 34 weaker ones can't decide anything on their own.

Where several sources agree on a pattern, that counts as evidence. Where only one says it, it's a lead to check.

㊩ (not saved yet) The regenerated graph is written over the old file in `storage/operator-turns/`; I kept the previous version at `/tmp/mined-pattern-graph.prev.json`. I haven't committed anything for this step.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (what the graph has) The graph is `storage/operator-turns/mined-pattern-graph.json`, built by `futon3c/scripts/mined_pattern_graph.py` and last generated on 30 September. Its giant component has 621 of 912 patterns. The edges come from operator-turn analyses: why, how, co-cited, rejected-beside and next-in-session. Each R-number usually has an `aif/…` pattern, a `problems/rN-…` pattern and sometimes a `war-room/…` one.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (how the third route would work) For each sampled pattern, look at which R-tagged patterns are within one or two steps, and weight the nearer ones more. That gives each pattern a spread over R-numbers from graph position alone, with no agents involved. The graph records how patterns come up together in your turns, while the turn bids record what you do in a turn. So the two routes are fairly independent. One caution on edge types: next-in-session is the largest (1,712 edges) and the weakest, so I'd compute one version with all edges and one with only why, how and co-cited.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (gaps the graph can't cover) R1 and R7 sit outside the giant component, and R3a and TRACE have no edges, so for those four the turn bids will be the only evidence. The graph is also a day old. I'd regenerate it first; `mined_pattern_graph.py` is a registered command, so that's cheap.
